newsitem.title: UK: UK PMI survey unlikely to hinder early rate rise.
newsitem.headline: UK PMI survey unlikely to hinder early rate rise.

text.p: A sharp fall in the UK purchasing managers' index in December is unlikely to silence calls for a rate rise early in the new year and analysts said the chances of a quarter-point increase in January are still high. "The authorities will find it useful to look at the effect sterling's strength is having on the sector, but the economy will still grow strongly this year, buoyed by consumers, and we expect a quarter point rate rise to follow the January meeting," said Philip Uglow, UK economist at Union Plc.

The overall index slipped to 52.5 percent from a downwardly revised 54.2 percent in November. The index level indicated expansion in the manufacturing economy, for the seventh month in succession, but the pace of growth eased.

The Chartered Institute of Purchasing and Supply (CIPS) which compiles the survey said the index was weakened by deceleration in the growth of order books prompted by the pound's recent appreciation and deliberate destocking by firms.
But Andrew Cates, UK economist at UBS, said the survey will do little to offset the Bank of England's fear that the economy is in danger of overheating.
"The message from the survey is that the recovery in the manufacturing economy is still very weak, but that is not the sector that the Bank of England is worried about," said Cates.
Bank officials have said they are concerned about the upswing in domestic demand which could allow retailers to raise their prices to restore margins.
But Cates said any request from the Bank of England for higher rates on January 15 may be overruled in favour of a move in February.
The recovery in Britain's manufacturing sector badly lags activity in the lively pick up consumer sector which is driving economic growth.
And just as manufacturing was showing signs of recovery in the autumn, sterling's dramatic appreciation choked off demand for British goods abroad.
But sterling's rally has also helped keep price pressures subdued.
"Sterling's appreciation is also helping to ensure that inflationary pressures in the industry remain extremely weak," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets.
The prices index edged down to 42.2 percent from 42.5 percent in November.
CIPS said reported upward price pressures in recent months, prompted by stronger demand for goods, were more than offset by the deflationary effect of sterling's strength.

Loynes said while the weaker prices index could help strengthen the case for rates to be left on hold, it was likely to be overshadowned by data covering consumer activity over the Christmas period, expected to be strong.
